\chapter{Friend, Family, Brother, and Sister}
\label{ch:bn-friend-family-brother-sister}
\hlchaptermodality{11}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name a friend, my family, my brother and my sister in Bengali, none of them marked for gender, and say which are borrowed whole from Sanskrit and which evolved by sound change, including one that turns out to share a root with the previous chapter's rice.}

The chapter closes on \bn{বোন}, which is not related to English 'sister' at all: it traces through Sanskrit bhaginī and bhaga, 'a share,' back to the same √bhaj that named Chapter 10's \bn{ভাত}. The reader names all four people (bôndhu, pôribār, bhāi, bon), states which two are tatsamas kept whole from Sanskrit (\bn{বন্ধু}, \bn{পরিবার}) and which two are tadbhavas worn down by sound change (\bn{ভাই}, \bn{বোন}), and counts a sibling or two using Chapter 6's numbers. It reaches back to rescue all five of Chapter 6's numbers atoms, unrevisited since the chapter that introduced them.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[bôndhu]{\bn{বন্ধু} (bôndhu) — \textquotedblleft{}friend,\textquotedblright{} someone you are bound to}

\label{lesson:BN-C11-bondhu}



\begin{quote}
Chapter 2 taught you to exchange names. This chapter names the people themselves — starting with the one whose acquaintance you were glad to make.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \bn{বন্ধু}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{বন্ধু}} — \emph{bôndhu} — \textbf{friend}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\bn{আমার} \bn{বন্ধু}} (\emph{āmār bôndhu}) — my friend. One word, whether that friend is a man or a woman: Chapter 7 already told you Bengali carries no grammatical gender on its verbs, its adjectives, or its nouns, and \bn{বন্ধু} is the plainest place to feel it — no ending changes, no second word to learn.

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\bn{বন্ধু}} is \textbf{\bn{ব}} (\emph{bô}) + \textbf{\bn{ন্ধ}} (\emph{ndhô}, a conjunct: \bn{ন} joined to the breathy dental \bn{ধ}) + \textbf{\bn{ু}} (\emph{u}). The conjunct is two consonants pressed together with no vowel between them, said as one cluster: \emph{n-dhu}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\bn{বন্ধু}} is Sanskrit \textbf{\bn{বন্ধু}} (\emph{bandhu}), kept essentially whole rather than worn down the way \bn{চা} or \bn{ভাত} were — Bengali took this one straight from Sanskrit rather than inheriting it through centuries of sound change. It is built on \textbf{√\bn{বন্ধ্}} (\emph{√bandh}, \textquotedblleft{}to bind, to tie\textquotedblright{}), from PIE \textbf{*b\textsuperscript{h}end\textsuperscript{h}-} — and here, unusually, the English cousin is not buried: \textbf{bind}, \textbf{bond} and \textbf{band} all come from the very same root. Bengali did not need to explain what a friend is; the word does it for you. A \bn{বন্ধু} is, at the root, someone you are bound to.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}bôndhu\textquotedblright{} — friend
  \item \textquotedblleft{}āmār bôndhu\textquotedblright{} — my friend, no gender marked either way
  \item the root, and its English family — \textquotedblleft{}bandh … bind, bond, band\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give \textquotedblleft{}my friend\textquotedblright{} in Bengali. (\textbf{\bn{আমার} \bn{বন্ধু}.}) What root is \bn{বন্ধু} built on, and which English words share it? (\textbf{√bandh, \textquotedblleft{}to bind\textquotedblright{}} — \textbf{bind}, \textbf{bond}, \textbf{band}.) Is \bn{বন্ধু} a word Bengali inherited through sound change, or one it kept whole from Sanskrit? (\textbf{Kept whole} — a tatsama.) Does \bn{বন্ধু} change for a friend who is a woman? (\textbf{No} — Chapter 7 already told you why: no grammatical gender, anywhere in the language.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[pôribār]{\bn{পরিবার} (pôribār) — \textquotedblleft{}family,\textquotedblright{} what surrounds you}

\label{lesson:BN-C11-poribar}



\begin{quote}
Last lesson named one person you are bound to. This one names the whole group.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \bn{পরিবার}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{পরিবার}} — \emph{pôribār} — \textbf{family}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\bn{আমার} \bn{পরিবার}} (\emph{āmār pôribār}) — my family.

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\bn{পরিবার}} is \textbf{\bn{প}} (\emph{pô}) + \textbf{\bn{রি}} (\emph{ri}) + \textbf{\bn{বা}} (\emph{bā}) + \textbf{\bn{র}} (\emph{r}, silent at the end, a bare consonant with nothing written after it). Four syllables in the spelling, three said aloud: \emph{pô-ri-bār}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\bn{পরিবার}} is Sanskrit \textbf{\bn{পরিবার}} (\emph{parivāra}), a second word Bengali kept whole from Sanskrit rather than letting it wear down — like \bn{বন্ধু}, another tatsama. It is built from \textbf{pari-}, \textquotedblleft{}around, about\textquotedblright{} (PIE \textbf{*peri-}, the same prefix English itself borrowed for \textbf{peri-meter} and \textbf{peri-phery}), plus \textbf{√\bn{বৃ}} (\emph{√vṛ}, \textquotedblleft{}to cover, to surround,\textquotedblright{} PIE \textbf{*h\textsubscript{2}wer-}). That root's secure cousins are Latin \emph{operiō}, \textquotedblleft{}to cover,\textquotedblright{} and Lithuanian \emph{suverti}, \textquotedblleft{}to shut\textquotedblright{} — no English word is claimed here, since none is secure. Put the pieces together and a \bn{পরিবার} is, at the root, \textbf{what stands around you and covers you}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}pôribār\textquotedblright{} — family
  \item \textquotedblleft{}āmār pôribār\textquotedblright{} — my family
  \item the two pieces — \textquotedblleft{}pari-, around … vṛ, to cover\textquotedblright{}
  \item a friend, then a family — \textquotedblleft{}bôndhu … pôribār\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give \textquotedblleft{}my family\textquotedblright{} in Bengali. (\textbf{\bn{আমার} \bn{পরিবার}.}) What does \bn{পরিবার} mean at the root, piece by piece? (\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}Around\textquotedblright{} plus \textquotedblleft{}to cover\textquotedblright{} — what surrounds and covers you.}) Does its root vṛ have a secure English cousin? (\textbf{No} — the secure cousins are Latin and Lithuanian.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[bhāi]{\bn{ভাই} (bhāi) — \textquotedblleft{}brother,\textquotedblright{} which never stopped being the word \textquotedblleft{}brother\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:BN-C11-bhai}



\begin{quote}
Two tatsamas so far, both kept whole from Sanskrit. This one took the other road — worn down by sound change until it barely looks related to where it started. Except it does.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \bn{ভাই}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{ভাই}} — \emph{bhāi} — \textbf{brother}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\bn{আমার} \bn{ভাই}} (\emph{āmār bhāi}) — my brother.

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\bn{ভাই}} is \textbf{\bn{ভা}} (\emph{bhā}, the breathy \emph{b} from \bn{ভাত} and \bn{ভালো}) plus \textbf{\bn{ই}} (\emph{i}), a full vowel letter rather than a sign — the two vowels run together into one syllable, \emph{bhāi}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\bn{ভাই}} is Sanskrit \textbf{\bn{ভ্রাতৃ}} (\emph{bhrātṛ}), worn down through Magadhi Prakrit \emph{bhāi} — a \textbf{tadbhava} this time, not a tatsama like \bn{বন্ধু} and \bn{পরিবার}: Bengali inherited this one through centuries of sound change rather than lifting it whole. And PIE \textbf{*b\textsuperscript{h}réh\textsubscript{2}tēr} sits behind \emph{bhrātṛ}, the same root that gives English \textbf{brother}, Latin \textbf{frāter} and Greek \textbf{phrátēr}. Nothing here is a cousin standing in for the real thing: \bn{ভাই} and \textquotedblleft{}brother\textquotedblright{} are, six thousand years apart, \textbf{the same word}.

Bengali also uses family words to address people outside the family: an older man might be called \textbf{\bn{দাদা}} (\emph{dādā}, \textquotedblleft{}elder brother\textquotedblright{}) as a mark of respect, whether or not he is any relation at all. That is a light touch on a habit this chapter will not turn into a system — but it is worth naming, since it means \bn{বন্ধু} and \bn{ভাই} are not always as far apart as they look.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}bhāi\textquotedblright{} — brother
  \item \textquotedblleft{}āmār bhāi\textquotedblright{} — my brother
  \item the same word, two languages — \textquotedblleft{}bhrātṛ … brother\textquotedblright{}
  \item friend, family, brother — \textquotedblleft{}bôndhu … pôribār … bhāi\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give \textquotedblleft{}my brother\textquotedblright{} in Bengali. (\textbf{\bn{আমার} \bn{ভাই}.}) Is \bn{ভাই} a cousin of English \textquotedblleft{}brother,\textquotedblright{} or the same word by descent? (\textbf{The same word} — PIE \emph{b\textsuperscript{h}réh\textsubscript{2}tēr}, no invention needed.) Is \bn{ভাই} a tatsama like \bn{বন্ধু} and \bn{পরিবার}, or a tadbhava? (\textbf{A tadbhava} — worn down through Prakrit, not kept whole.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[bon]{\bn{বোন} (bon) — \textquotedblleft{}sister,\textquotedblright{} and the root it shares with rice}

\label{lesson:BN-C11-bon}



\begin{quote}
\bn{ভাই} (\emph{bhāi}) turned out to be the very word \textquotedblleft{}brother.\textquotedblright{} This one does not — and where it comes from instead is the surprise this chapter has been saving.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \bn{বোন}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{বোন}} — \emph{bon} — \textbf{sister}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\bn{আমার} \bn{বোন}} (\emph{āmār bon}) — my sister.

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\bn{বোন}} is \textbf{\bn{ব}} with the vowel sign \textbf{\bn{ো}} (\emph{bo}) plus \textbf{\bn{ন}} (\emph{n}), silent at the end — one plain consonant, no cluster, so the inherent vowel drops just as it did on \bn{দুধ} and \bn{ভাত}: \emph{bon}, not \emph{bono}.

\begin{cousinweb}
English \textquotedblleft{}sister\textquotedblright{} descends from PIE \textbf{*swésōr}. \textbf{\bn{বোন} does not.} It is a tadbhava through Magadhi Prakrit \emph{*bahiṇī, from Old Indo-Aryan }*baghinī — a doublet of Sanskrit's own \textbf{\bn{ভগিনী}} (\emph{bhaginī}), \textquotedblleft{}one with a share,\textquotedblright{} built on \textbf{\bn{ভগ}} (\emph{bhaga}), \textquotedblleft{}a share, a portion, good fortune.\textquotedblright{} And \emph{bhaga} is a noun from the very same verb that named this chapter's rice two lessons ago: \textbf{√\bn{ভজ্}} (\emph{√bhaj}, \textquotedblleft{}to divide, to share out\textquotedblright{}), PIE \textbf{*b\textsuperscript{h}eh\textsubscript{2}g-}. \bn{ভাত} is \textquotedblleft{}the portion given\textquotedblright{}; \bn{বোন} is \textquotedblleft{}the one with a portion.\textquotedblright{} Bengali's word for sister and Bengali's word for rice are, underneath, cousins. Its word for sister and English's are not.

The same light touch as last lesson's \bn{দাদা} applies here: an older woman may be addressed as \textbf{\bn{দিদি}} (\emph{didi}, \textquotedblleft{}elder sister\textquotedblright{}) as a mark of respect, family or not.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}bon\textquotedblright{} — sister, no trailing vowel
  \item \textquotedblleft{}āmār bon\textquotedblright{} — my sister
  \item the shared root — \textquotedblleft{}bhaj … bhāt, bon\textquotedblright{}
  \item all four of this chapter's people — \textquotedblleft{}bôndhu, pôribār, bhāi, bon\textquotedblright{}
  \item a count of them, using Chapter 6's numbers — \textquotedblleft{}āmār ek bhāi. āmār dui bon.\textquotedblright{} — one brother. two sisters.
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Is \bn{বোন} related to English \textquotedblleft{}sister\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{No} — different root entirely.) What is it related to instead? (\textbf{\bn{ভাত}} — both trace to √bhaj, \textquotedblleft{}to share.\textquotedblright{}) Say \textquotedblleft{}one brother\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}two sisters.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Ek bhāi. Dui bon.}) Which of those two numbers keeps a vowel Hindi and Marathi lost? (\textbf{\bn{দুই}} — the \emph{-i} after the old \emph{dv-}.) And which number wears the chandrabindu? (\textbf{\bn{পাঁচ}}, five — not needed here, but still the only one that has it.)
\end{tcolorbox}
